title: Promises that cannot be taken literally
source_text: Ἀλλὰ καὶ εἴπερ δυναστεύειν αὐτοῖς ὁ νόμος ἐπηγγέλλετο λέγων· „ἄρξεις σὺ [δὲ] ἐθνῶν πολλῶν, σοῦ δὲ οὐκ ἄρξουσι,“ καὶ μηδὲν δηλοῦται διὰ τούτων βαθύτερον, δῆλον ὅτι πολλῷ πλέον κατεγίνωσκεν ὁ λαὸς τῶν κατὰ τὸν νόμον ἐπαγγελιῶν. παραφράζει δέ τινας λέξεις ὁ Κέλσος, ἐμφαινούσας πληρωθήσεσθαι πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν διὰ τοῦ Ἑβραϊκοῦ σπέρματος· ὅπερ ὡς πρὸς τὴν ἱστορίαν μηνίοντος, ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω, τοῦ θεοῦ γεγένηται μετὰ τὴν Ἰησοῦ ἐπιδημίαν ἤπερ εὐλογίας ἀποδιδόντος. ἀλλὰ καὶ περὶ τοῦ ἐν ἐπαγγελίᾳ εἰρῆσθαι Ἰουδαίοις καταφονεύειν τοὺς πολεμίους λεκτέον (ὅτι) , εἴ τις ἀναλέγοιτο καὶ προσέχοι ἐπιμελῶς ταῖς λέξεσιν, εὕροι ἂν ἀδύνατον εἶναι τὴν ὡς πρὸς τὸ ῥητὸν ἐκδοχήν. ἀρκεῖ δ᾿ ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος ἀπὸ τῶν ψαλμῶν παραθέσθαι, τίνα τρόπον ὁ δίκαιος εἰσάγεται λέγων πρὸς ἑτέροις καὶ τό· „εἰς τὰς πρωΐας ἀπέκτεινον πάντας τοὺς ἁμαρτωλοὺς τῆς γῆς, τοῦ ἐξολοθρεῦσαι ἐκ πόλεως κυρίου πάντας τοὺς ἐργαζομένους τὴν ἀνομίαν.“ πρόσχες δὴ τῷ ῥητῷ καὶ τῇ διαθέσει τοῦ λέγοντος, εἰ ἐδύνατο ἀνδραγαθήματα προδιηγησάμενος, ἅπερ ἔκκειται τῷ βουλομένῳ ἀναγινώσκειν, ἐπιφέρειν τὸ ὡς πρὸς τὴν λέξιν δυνατὸν, ὅτι οὐκ ἄλλῳ καιρῷ τῆς ἡμέρας ἢ τῷ ἑωθινῷ ἀνῄρει „πάντας τοὺς ἁμαρτωλοὺς τῆς γῆς,“ ὡς μηδένα καταλιπεῖν αὐτῶν ζῶντα· καὶ εἰ ἐξωλόθρευεν ἀπὸ τῆς Ἱερουσαλὴμ πάνθ᾿ ὁντινοῦν ἄνθρωπον ἐργαζόμενον „τὴν ἀνομίαν.“ πολλὰ δ᾿ ἂν εὕροις καὶ ἐν τῷ νόμῳ τοιαῦτα ὡς τὸ „οὐ κατελίπομεν αὐτῶν ζωγρίαν.“
pass_a_gloss: But also if the law promised (ἐπαγγέλλομαι) them to hold power (δυναστεύω), saying 'you will rule (ἄρχω) many nations, but they will not rule you', and nothing deeper (βαθύτερον) is shown (δηλόω) through these, it is clear that the people would have condemned (καταγιγνώσκω) much more the promises (ἐπαγγελίαι) according to the law. Celsus paraphrases (παραφράζω) certain words (λέξεις) indicating (ἐμφαίνω) that all the earth will be filled (πληρόω) through the Hebrew seed (σπέρμα); which, as regards the history (ἱστορία), has happened after the coming (ἐπιδημία) of Jesus, God being wrathful (μηνίω), that I may so name it, rather than giving back blessing (εὐλογία). But also about its having been said in promise to Jews to slaughter (καταφονεύω) the enemies it must be said that, if one should read (ἀναλέγομαι) and attend (προσέχω) carefully (ἐπιμελῶς) to the words, he would find the interpretation (ἐκδοχή) according to the spoken letter (ῥητόν) impossible (ἀδύνατον). It suffices (ἀρκεῖ) for the present to set alongside (παρατίθημι) from the psalms in what way (τρόπος) the just man is introduced (εἰσάγω) saying, besides other things, also: 'in the mornings (πρωΐαι) I killed (ἀποκτείνω) all the sinners (ἁμαρτωλοί) of the earth, to destroy utterly (ἐξολοθρεύω) from the city of the Lord all those working (ἐργάζομαι) lawlessness (ἀνομία)'. Attend then to the letter and to the disposition (διάθεσις) of the speaker, whether, having narrated beforehand (προδιηγέομαι) brave deeds (ἀνδραγαθήματα), which are set out (ἔκκειμαι) for the one wishing to read, he was able to add (ἐπιφέρω) the [thing] possible as to the wording, that at no other time (καιρός) of the day than the dawn (ἑωθινός) he slew (ἀναιρέω) all the sinners of the earth, so as to leave (καταλείπω) none of them living; and whether he utterly destroyed from Jerusalem every man whatsoever working lawlessness. You would find many such things also in the law, like 'we did not leave of them a captive alive (ζωγρία)'.
pass_b_english: Moreover, if the law promised them dominion when it said, “You shall rule over many nations, but they shall not rule over you” (Deuteronomy 15:6), and nothing deeper is meant by these words, it is clear that the people would have condemned the promises of the law all the more. Celsus paraphrases certain words which suggest that the whole earth will be filled by the Hebrew seed. As a matter of history, this has come about after the coming of Jesus, because God was angry, if I may use that word, rather than because he was granting a blessing.

As for its being said to the Jews, by way of promise, that they would slaughter their enemies, we must say that anyone who reads and attends carefully to the words would find the literal interpretation impossible. For the present it is enough to cite from the Psalms the way in which the righteous man is introduced as saying, among other things, this too: “In the mornings I killed all the sinners of the earth, to destroy from the city of the Lord all who work lawlessness” (Psalm 101:8).

Consider, then, the wording and the frame of mind of the speaker. After first telling of virtuous deeds, which lie open to anyone who wishes to read them, could he go on to state, as something literally possible, that at no other time of day than the early morning he slew “all the sinners of the earth”, so as to leave none of them alive? And did he really destroy from Jerusalem every single man who worked “lawlessness”? And you would find many such sayings in the law as well, such as “We did not leave any of them alive” (Deuteronomy 2:34).

choices.choice: Brackets in Koetschau: [δὲ] in the Deuteronomy quotation is deleted by the editor and not translated; (ὅτι) is an editorial supplement, followed. LXX renumbering: Psalm 100:8 LXX = Psalm 101:8 English. γῆ rendered ‘earth’ (not ‘land’) because Origen in 7.22 interprets ‘earth’ figuratively as the flesh. ‘From Jerusalem’ is Origen’s own gloss on ‘the city of the Lord’. ‘Virtuous deeds’ (ἀνδραγαθήματα, ‘brave or noble deeds’): Origen refers to what the psalmist recounts before verse 8, which in Psalm 101 is a ruler’s upright conduct, so ‘virtuous’ fits better than ‘brave’. The two εἰ clauses (‘whether he could add ... and whether he destroyed’) are turned into two direct questions; the second asks whether the literal sense could be true. ‘We did not leave any of them alive’: ζωγρία (‘a captive taken alive’) matches LXX Deuteronomy 2:34 (οὐ κατελίπομεν ζωγρείαν); compare Deuteronomy 3:3 and Joshua 10:28–40. Uncited: the earth filled by ‘the Hebrew seed’ refers to texts Celsus paraphrased (seed promises such as Genesis 22:17; 28:14); Origen’s point is that the Jewish dispersion after Jesus came as wrath, not blessing. ‘If I may use that word’ (ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω) marks Origen’s hesitation in attributing anger to God.
genitive absolute μηνίοντος ... ἤπερ εὐλογίας ἀποδιδόντος: 'with God angry ... rather than bestowing blessing' -> 'because God was angry ... rather than because he was granting a blessing'
ἀνδραγαθήματα: 'brave deeds' -> 'virtuous deeds' (Psalm 101 recounts upright conduct)
τὸ ὡς πρὸς τὴν λέξιν δυνατόν: 'something that is possible taken literally' read as if the literal sense were possible; now 'as something literally possible', as a question
second εἰ clause now its own question ('And did he really destroy from Jerusalem ...?')
citations checked: Deuteronomy 15:6 (LXX ἄρξεις σὺ ἐθνῶν πολλῶν), Psalm 101:8 (LXX 100:8), Deuteronomy 2:34 (LXX οὐ κατελίπομεν ζωγρείαν)
